L138: 
L139: The projectively dual variety of $X$ is defined as ${X^{\vee}\coloneqq\overline{\mathrm{pr}_{2}(\mathrm{Con}(X^{\rm sm}))}}$.
L140: 
L144: If $\operatorname{codim}(X^{\vee})>1$, we call $X$ defective and set $\Delta_{X}=1$. Returning to the conormal variety, we list some of its most important properties. A fundamental result is biduality: $\mathcal{N}_{X}=\mathcal{N}_{X^{\vee}}$. Recall now that the cohomology ring of $\mathbb{P}^{n}\times(\mathbb{P}^{n})^{\vee}$ is a truncated polynomial ring
L145: 
L146:  | $$H^{*}(\mathbb{P}^{n}\times(\mathbb{P}^{n})^{\vee},\mathbb{Z})\simeq\mathbb{Z}[s,t]/(s^{n+1},t^{n+1}),$$  |
L147: where $s$ and $t$ denote the hyperplane classes pulled back from the first and second factors, respectively. The cohomology class of $\mathcal{N}_{X}$ in $H^{*}(\mathbb{P}^{n}\times(\mathbb{P}^{n})^{\vee},\mathbb{Z})$ is given by the bilinear form
L148: 
L149:  | $$[\mathcal{N}_{X}]=\delta_{1}(X)\,s^{n}t+\delta_{2}(X)\,s^{n-1}t^{2}+\cdots+\delta_{n}(X)\,s\,t^{n}.$$  |
L150: 
L151: The integers $\delta_{i}(X)$ are called the polar degrees of $X$. They are positive if and only if
L152:  | $$\operatorname{codim}(X^{\vee})\leq i\leq\dim(X)+1.$$  |
L153: 
L154: Moreover, $\delta_{\dim(X)+1}=\deg(X)$ and $\delta_{\operatorname{codim}(X^{\vee})}=\deg(X^{\vee})$; for further properties see [cite45†42 ].
L155: Finally, we recall the notion of higher associated hypersurfaces of $X$. Let $\mathrm{Gr}(\ell,\mathbb{P}^{n})$ denote the Grassmannian parametrizing linear spaces of projective dimension $\ell$ in $\mathbb{P}^{n}$. For such linear space $L\in\mathrm{Gr}(\ell,\mathbb{P}^{n})$, take a matrix $A\in\mathbb{C}^{(n-\ell)\times(n+1)}$ such that
L156: 
L157:  | $$L=\mathbb{P}(\ker(A)).$$  |
L158: The entries of $A$ are called the Stiefel coordinates of $L$, and the maximal minors $p_{i_{1}\cdots i_{n-\ell}}$ of $A$ are its Plücker coordinates. Note that the Plücker coordinates are uniquely determined up to a common scalar factor, whereas the Stiefel coordinates are not. Indeed, left multiplication of $A$ by any invertible $(n-\ell)\times(n-\ell)$ matrix does not change its kernel.
L159: The dual variety $X^{\vee}$ records hyperplanes tangent to $X^{\mathrm{sm}}$, equivalently, hyperplanes whose intersection with $X$ is non-transverse. This idea extends to linear spaces of arbitrary dimension.
L160: ###### Definition 2.4.
L161: 
L162: For $i\in\{0,\dots,d\}$, define the higher associated variety of $X$ as
L163: 
L164:  | $$\mathcal{Z}_{i}(X)\coloneqq\overline{\bigl\{L\in\mathrm{Gr}(n-d+i-1,\mathbb{P}^{n})\mid\exists\,x\in X^{\mathrm{sm}}\cap L:\ \dim(L\cap T_{x}X)\geq i\bigr\}}.$$  |  | (6)
L165: Notice that for $i=d$, the variety $\mathcal{Z}_{d}(X)$ is exactly the projective dual variety $X^{\vee}\subset(\mathbb{P}^{n})^{\vee}$. We will focus on the case when $\mathcal{Z}_{i}(X)$ is a hypersurface in $\mathrm{Gr}(n-d+i-1,\mathbb{P}^{n})$. This happens precisely when $i\leq\dim(X)-\operatorname{codim}(X^{\vee})+1$. For $i=0$, $\mathcal{Z}_{0}(X)$ is the Chow hypersurface of $X$, consisting of linear spaces $L\in\mathrm{Gr}(n-d-1,\mathbb{P}^{n})$ that meet $X$.
L166: Its defining equation in Plücker coordinates has degree $\deg X$ and is called the Chow form of $X$. For $i=1$, $\mathcal{Z}_{1}(X)$ is the Hurwitz variety, parametrizing linear spaces $L\in\mathrm{Gr}(n-d,\mathbb{P}^{n})$ that meet $X$ non-transversely. When $\deg X>1$, it is a hypersurface and its defining equation is called the Hurwitz form of $X$.
L167: ### Whitney Stratifications
L168: 
L169: Whitney stratifications will be one of the main tools we will use in what follows. We introduce them briefly in this section. For more details, we refer to the textbooks [cite46†17 , cite47†29 ].
L170: 
L171: A stratification of $X$ is a finite partition $\mathcal{S}=\{S_{\alpha}\}_{\alpha\in A}$ of $X$ into smooth locally closed subvarieties, called strata, such that for every $\alpha\in A$, the boundary $\overline{S_{\alpha}}\setminus S_{\alpha}$ is a union of strata.
L172: ###### Definition 2.5.
L173: 
L174: A stratification $\mathcal{S}$ is called a Whitney stratification if for every pair of strata satisfying $S_{\beta}\subset\overline{S_{\alpha}}\setminus S_{\alpha}$ the following conditions hold:
L175: 
L176:   1. (a)
L177: 
L178: for every sequence $(x_{n})\subset S_{\alpha}$ with $x_{n}\to x\in S_{\beta}$ and $T_{x_{n}}S_{\alpha}\to T$, one has $T_{x}S_{\beta}\subseteq T$;
L179: 
L180:   2. (b)
L181: for every pair of sequences $(x_{n})\subset S_{\alpha}$, $(y_{n})\subset S_{\beta}$ with $x_{n},y_{n}\to x\in S_{\beta}$, if the secant lines $\overline{x_{n}y_{n}}$ converge to a line $\ell$ and the tangent planes $T_{x_{n}}S_{\alpha}$ converge to $T$, then $\ell\subseteq T$.
L182: A Whitney stratification is called minimal (or coarsest) if, after merging any number of strata, the resulting stratification no longer satisfies the above conditions. A fundamental theorem is that every complex algebraic variety admits a unique minimal Whitney stratification, see [cite48†65 , cite26†62 , cite49†49 ].
L183: When a closed subvariety $Y\subset X$ is fixed, by a minimal Whitney stratification compatible with $Y$ we mean a coarsest Whitney stratification of $X$ refining the partition $X=(X\setminus Y)\sqcup Y.$ Equivalently, the subvariety $Y$ is required to be a union of strata.
L184: ###### Definition 2.6.
L185: 
L186: A Whitney stratification of a morphism $f:X\to Y$ is a pair of Whitney stratifications $\mathcal{S}_{X}$ of $X$ and $\mathcal{T}_{Y}$ of $Y$ such that for every stratum $S\in\mathcal{S}_{X}$ there exists a stratum $T\in\mathcal{T}_{Y}$ such that $f(S)\subseteq T$ and the restriction $f|_{S}:S\to T$ is a submersion onto its image.
L187: Whitney stratifications of maps always exist, see Theorem 1 in Section 4 of [cite50†35 ]. For checking Whitney regularity, the Lê-Teissier conormal criterion [cite27†44 ] provides an algebraic test. Effective algorithms for computing Whitney stratifications are given in [cite51†32 , cite52†31 ].
L188: ###### Remark 2.7.
L189: 
L190: We note that Whitney stratifications are more common in the study of complex analytic spaces, that is, complex spaces where singularities are allowed. These are more general than complex algebraic varieties, since they are locally defined by holomorphic functions rather than polynomials. They are naturally endowed with the Euclidean topology.
L191: However, throughout, we identify complex algebraic varieties with their associated analytic spaces whenever we discuss limits of points or tangent spaces, and Whitney conditions. Indeed, for constructible subsets of a complex algebraic variety, Euclidean and Zariski closure have the same underlying set. Therefore, points in the Zariski closure of a constructible set may be approached by sequences of complex points from that set.
L192: Conversely, by Chow’s theorem [cite53†14 ], closed analytic subsets of a complex projective variety are also Zariski closed.
L193: ###### Remark 2.8.
L194: 
L195: We will use two standard properties of Whitney stratifications. First, if $\mathcal{S}=\{S_{\alpha}\}$ and $\mathcal{T}=\{T_{\beta}\}$ are some Whitney stratifications of $X$ and $Y$, respectively, then
L196: 
L197:  | $$\mathcal{S}\times\mathcal{T}=\{S_{\alpha}\times T_{\beta}\}_{\alpha,\beta}$$  |
L198: is a Whitney stratification of $X\times Y$. In particular, if $Y$ is smooth, then $\{S_{\alpha}\times Y\}_{\alpha}$ is a Whitney stratification of $X\times Y$. Second, if $Z\subset X$ is a smooth subvariety transverse to all strata $S_{\alpha}$, then the nonempty intersections $S_{\alpha}\cap Z$ form a Whitney stratification of $X\cap Z$. These facts are direct consequences of the definition; see, for example, [cite54†27 , pp. 12-13].
L199: ## 3. Dualizing Flat Families
L200: 
L201: In this section we study the behavior of projective duality under flat degenerations of ${X\subset\mathbb{P}^{n}}$.
L202: For the rest of this section, take $\mathbb{A}^{1}=\mathrm{Spec}\,\mathbb{C}[t]$ and let $\mathcal{X}\subseteq\mathbb{P}^{n}\times\mathbb{A}^{1}$ be a reduced, irreducible closed subscheme, flat over $\mathbb{A}^{1}$ with the projection denoted by $\pi:\mathcal{X}\rightarrow\mathbb{A}^{1}$. We write $\mathcal{I}\subseteq\mathbb{C}[t,y]$ for its vanishing ideal, homogeneous in $y=(y_{0},\ldots,y_{n})$, and $X_{t}:=\pi^{-1}(t)$ for the fiber over $t\in\mathbb{A}^{1}$.
L203: Additionally, we assume that general fibers $X_{t}$ for $t\neq 0$ are reduced.
L204: The degeneration of $X$ induces a degeneration of the conormal variety $\mathcal{N}_{X}$. The latter construction has already appeared in greater generality in the analytic setting under the name of the relative conormal space of a map, see [cite55†45 , Section 1.6], and also [cite26†62 , cite27†44 , cite56†25 ].
L205: ###### Definition 3.1.
L206: 
L207: The conormal space $\mathcal{N}_{\mathcal{X}/\mathbb{A}^{1}}$ relative to $\pi$ is the scheme-theoretic closure of the set of triples $(x,H,\pi(x))$ such that $x$ is a smooth point of the general fiber $\pi^{-1}(\pi(x))$ and $H$ is a tangent hyperplane to $\pi^{-1}(\pi(x))$ at $x$. In symbols, we have
L208:  | $$\mathcal{N}_{\mathcal{X}/\mathbb{A}^{1}}:=\overline{\bigcup_{t\in\mathbb{A}^{1}\setminus\{0\}}\mathrm{Con}(X_{t}^{\rm sm})}\subseteq\mathbb{P}^{n}\times(\mathbb{P}^{n})^{\vee}\times\mathbb{A}^{1}.$$  |  | (7)
L209: ###### Remark 3.2.
L210: 
L211: Similarly to Remark cite57†2.2 , we can write down the defining ideal of $\mathcal{N}_{\mathcal{X}/\mathbb{A}^{1}}$. Let $J_{y}$ be the Jacobian matrix of the ideal $\mathcal{I}$ with respect to the $y$-variables and consider the augmented Jacobian matrix $M_{y}=\binom{z}{J_{y}}$. Then,
L212: 
L213:  | $$I_{\mathcal{N}_{\mathcal{X}/\mathbb{A}^{1}}}=\sqrt{\Bigl(\bigl(\mathcal{I}+I_{c+1}(M_{y})\bigr):\bigl(\mathcal{I}+I_{c}(J_{y})\bigr)^{\infty}\Bigr):(z_{0},\dots,z_{n})^{\infty}},$$  |
L214: where $c={\rm codim}(X_{t})$ for $t\in\mathbb{A}^{1}$. Note that, by Remark cite58†3.4 , no saturation by $(t)$ is needed.
L215: ### The support of the limiting conormal cycle
L216: In what follows, Proposition cite30†3.3 and Theorem cite31†3.11 overlap with results in [cite28†41 ]. Kleiman showed that under a flat degeneration the conormal scheme specializes to a union of conormal schemes, with possible extra components lying over subvarieties of the singular locus of the special fiber. Here we refine the description of these extra components using Whitney stratifications, and we make the conormal degeneration explicit for Gröbner degenerations.
L217: ###### Proposition 3.3.
L218: 
L219: Let $\mathcal{X}\to\mathbb{A}^{1}$ be the Gröbner degeneration of $X\subset\mathbb{P}^{n}$ with respect to the weight $\omega$. Then the relative conormal space ${\cal N}_{\mathcal{X}/\mathbb{A}^{1}}$ is the Gröbner degeneration of the conormal variety ${\cal N}_{X}\subset\mathbb{P}^{n}\times(\mathbb{P}^{n})^{\vee}$ with respect to the weight $(\omega,-\omega)$. In particular,
L220:  | $${\cal N}_{X_{t}}=({\cal N}_{\mathcal{X}/\mathbb{A}^{1}})_{t}\hskip 10.00002pt\text{for every }t\in\mathbb{C}^{\times},$$  |
L221: 
L222: and, set-theoretically, we have the inclusion ${\cal N}_{X_{0}}\subseteq({\cal N}_{\mathcal{X}/\mathbb{A}^{1}})_{0}$.
L223: ###### Proof.
L224: 
L225: For $t\in\mathbb{C}^{\times}$, consider the following torus action on $\mathbb{P}^{n}\times(\mathbb{P}^{n})^{\vee}$:
L226: 
L227:  | $$\phi_{t}:(x,z)\mapsto(t^{\omega}\cdot x,t^{-\omega}\cdot z)\coloneq\bigl(\,[t^{\omega_{0}}x_{0}:\cdots:t^{\omega_{n}}x_{n}],\,[t^{-\omega_{0}}z_{0}:\cdots:t^{-\omega_{n}}z_{n}]\,\bigr).$$  |
L228: We show that $\phi_{t}({\rm Con}(X^{\rm sm}))={\rm Con}(X_{t}^{\rm sm})$. Indeed, consider a Gröbner basis $\{g_{1},\ldots,g_{r}\}$ of the vanishing ideal $I_{X}$ with respect to the weight $\omega$. Write $g_{\omega}^{t}(y)=t^{v(g)}g(t^{-\omega}\cdot y)$, where $v(g_{i})=\max_{\alpha\in\text{supp}(g_{i})}\{\langle\omega,\alpha\rangle\}$. The point $t^{\omega}\cdot x$ is in $X_{t}$ if and only if $x\in X$, since
L229:  | $$(g_{i})_{\omega}^{t}(t^{\omega}\cdot x)=t^{v(g_{i})}g_{i}(t^{-\omega}\cdot t^{\omega}\cdot x)=t^{v(g_{i})}g_{i}(x).$$  |
L230: 
L231: Moreover, the Jacobian matrix of $I_{X_{t}}$ at $t^{\omega}\cdot x$ is obtained from the Jacobian matrix of $I_{X}$ at $x$ by multiplying rows and columns by nonzero scalars. Thus both matrices have the same rank:
L232: 
L233:  | $$\frac{\partial(g_{i})_{\omega}^{t}}{\partial x_{j}}(t^{\omega}\cdot x)=t^{v(g_{i})-\omega_{j}}\frac{\partial g_{i}}{\partial x_{j}}(x).$$  |  | (8)
L234: In particular, smooth points of $X$ and of $X_{t}$ are in bijection under $x\mapsto t^{\omega}\cdot x$. Now let $(x,z)\in{\rm Con}(X^{\rm sm})$. By definition, $T_{x}X\subset H_{z}$. Equivalently, $z$ lies in the row span of the Jacobian matrix of $I_{X}$ at $x$. Then, by (cite59†8 ), the point $t^{-\omega}\cdot z$ lies in the row span of the Jacobian matrix of $X_{t}$ at $t^{\omega}\cdot x$. Hence, we have
L235:  | $$T_{t^{\omega}\cdot x}(X_{t})\subset H_{t^{-\omega}\cdot z}\hskip 10.00002pt\text{and}\hskip 10.00002pt(t^{\omega}\cdot x,t^{-\omega}\cdot z)\in{\rm Con}(X_{t}^{\rm sm}).$$  |
L236: 
L237: The same argument applied to the inverse rescaling gives the reverse inclusion. We obtain
L238: 
L239:  | $${\rm Con}(X_{t}^{\rm sm})=(t^{\omega},t^{-\omega})\cdot{\rm Con}(X^{\rm sm})\hskip 10.00002pt\forall\,t\neq 0.$$  |
L240: By definition, the closure of the LHS over all $t\in\mathbb{C}^{\times}$ is exactly the relative conormal ${\cal N}_{\mathcal{X}/\mathbb{A}^{1}}$, while the closure of the RHS gives the Gröbner degeneration of ${\cal N}_{X}$ with respect to the weight vector $(\omega,-\omega)$. Consequently, we have the equality $({\cal N}_{\mathcal{X}/\mathbb{A}^{1}})_{t}={\cal N}_{X_{t}}$ for every $t\in\mathbb{C}^{\times}$.
L241: To show the last statement, take $(x_{0},H_{0})\in\operatorname{Con}(X_{0}^{\rm sm})$. By definition, $x_{0}\in X_{0}^{\rm sm}$ and $T_{x_{0}}X_{0}\subset H_{0}$. We show that it is a limit of conormal points of the nearby fibers. Indeed, let $J(t,x)$ be the Jacobian matrix of the vanishing ideal of the fiber $X_{t}$, with respect to the fiber variables, as in Remark cite60†3.2 . Since $x_{0}\in X_{0}^{\rm sm}$, $J(0,x_{0})$ has the expected rank $\operatorname{codim}(X_{0})$.
L242: Hence, we may choose a curve $x(t)\in X_{t}^{\rm sm}$ with $x(0)=x_{0}$. Let $z_{0}$ define $H_{0}$. The condition $T_{x_{0}}X_{0}\subset H_{0}$ means that $z_{0}$ lies in the row span of $J(0,x_{0})$, so choose $\lambda$ with $z_{0}=\lambda^{\top}J(0,x_{0}).$ Set $z(t)=\lambda^{\top}J(t,x(t))$. Then $z(t)\to z_{0}$, and $z(t)$ lies in the row span of $J(t,x(t))$, hence
L243:  | $$T_{x(t)}X_{t}\subset H_{z(t)}\;\iff\;(x(t),H_{z(t)})\in\operatorname{Con}(X_{t}^{\rm sm})\hskip 10.00002pt\text{and}\hskip 10.00002pt(x(t),H_{z(t)})\to(x_{0},H_{0}).$$  |
L244: 
L245: Therefore $\operatorname{Con}(X_{0}^{\rm sm})\subseteq(\mathcal{N}_{\mathcal{X}/\mathbb{A}^{1}})_{0},$ and taking closures gives inclusion $\mathcal{N}_{X_{0}}\subseteq(\mathcal{N}_{\mathcal{X}/\mathbb{A}^{1}})_{0}$. ∎
L246: ###### Remark 3.4.
L247: 
L248: In the proof we showed that $\operatorname{Con}(X_{0}^{\rm sm})\subseteq(\mathcal{N}_{\mathcal{X}/\mathbb{A}^{1}})_{0}$. Hence, the closure in Definition cite61†3.1 may equivalently be taken over the whole line $\mathbb{A}^{1}$. Thus our definition agrees with the usual analytic definition of the relative conormal space, as in [cite26†62 , cite27†44 , cite56†25 ].

L250: The above proposition immediately implies the following statement for dual varieties.
L251: ###### Corollary 3.5.
L252: 
L253: A flat Gröbner degeneration of $X\subset\mathbb{P}^{n}$ with respect to the weight $\omega$ induces the flat Gröbner degeneration of $X^{\vee}\subset(\mathbb{P}^{n})^{\vee}$ with respect to the opposite weight $-\omega$. Moreover,
L254: 
L255:  | $$(X_{t})^{\vee}=(X^{\vee})_{t}\hskip 10.00002pt\text{for }\;t\neq 0,\hskip 10.00002pt\text{and}\hskip 10.00002pt(X_{0})^{\vee}\subseteq(X^{\vee})_{0}.$$  |
L256: If $\dim(X_{0})^{\vee}=\dim X^{\vee}$, then $\deg(X_{0})^{\vee}\leq\deg X^{\vee}$ with equality if and only if $(X_{0})^{\vee}=(X^{\vee})_{0}$.
L257: ###### Remark 3.6.
L258: Proposition cite30†3.3 and Corollary cite62†3.5 were proven for the vanishing locus of the projective varieties involved. Therefore, in the statements above, if the special fiber $X_{0}$ is non-reduced, then $\mathcal{N}_{X_{0}}$ and $X_{0}^{\vee}$ are understood as $\mathcal{N}_{X_{0}^{\mathrm{red}}}$ and $(X_{0}^{\mathrm{red}})^{\vee}$, respectively.
L259: Moreover, if $X_{0}$ is reducible, ${\cal N}_{X_{0}}$ or $X_{0}^{\vee}$ is the union of the conormal or dual varieties of the irreducible components of $(X_{0})^{\mathrm{red}}$. The scheme structure of $X_{0}$, however, still affects the multiplicities appearing in the limiting conormal cycle $[(\mathcal{N}_{\mathcal{X}/\mathbb{A}^{1}})_{0}]$, as we will explain in the next subsection.
L260: The inclusions in Proposition cite30†3.3 and Corollary cite62†3.5 are strict in general. The next example shows that the limit of the dual (and hence conormal) variety may have extra components.
L261: ###### Example 3.7.
L262: 
L263: Consider the family ${\cal X}={\cal V}(y_{1}^{2}y_{2}-y_{0}^{2}y_{3}+t^{2}(y_{3}^{3}+y_{2}^{3}))\subset\mathbb{P}^{3}\times\mathbb{A}^{1}$. This is the flat Gröbner degeneration of the smooth cubic with weight $\omega=(1,1,0,0)$. The special fiber is
L264: 
L265:  | $$X_{0}={\cal V}(y_{1}^{2}y_{2}-y_{0}^{2}y_{3}),$$  |
L266: known as the Whitney umbrella. Its dual $(X_{0})^{\vee}$ is given by ${\cal V}(z_{1}^{2}z_{2}+z_{0}^{2}z_{3})$, whereas the special fiber of the induced dual degeneration with respect to the weight $(-1,-1,0,0)$ is
L267: 
L268:  | $$(X^{\vee})_{0}={\cal V}\left(z_{3}^{3}z_{2}^{3}(z_{3}^{3}-z_{2}^{3})(z_{1}^{2}z_{2}+z_{0}^{2}z_{3})\right).$$  |  | (9)
L269: 
L270: Thus, we have strict inclusions: $(X_{0})^{\vee}\subsetneq(X^{\vee})_{0}$ and $\mathcal{N}_{X_{0}}\subsetneq(\mathcal{N}_{\mathcal{X}/\mathbb{A}^{1}})_{0}$. $\diamond$
L271: The extra factors in Example cite63†3.7 come from subvarieties of the singular locus of the special fiber $X_{0}$. We now introduce the tool which will allow us to identify these subvarieties.
L272: ###### Definition 3.8.
L273: 
L274: [Thom’s $a_{\pi}$-condition] Let $\mathcal{S}$ be a stratification of the map $\pi:{\mathcal{X}\to\mathbb{A}^{1}}$. We say that $\mathcal{S}$ satisfies Thom’s $a_{\pi}$-condition if, for every pair of strata satisfying $S_{\beta}\subset\overline{S_{\alpha}}\setminus S_{\alpha}$, every point $x\in S_{\beta}$, and every sequence $(x_{n})\in S_{\alpha}$ with $x_{n}\to x$, we have
L275:  | $$\text{if }\;T_{x_{n}}\bigl(S_{\alpha}\cap X_{\pi(x_{n})}\bigr)\to T,\hskip 10.00002pt\text{then }\;T_{x}\bigl(S_{\beta}\cap X_{\pi(x)}\bigr)\subseteq T.$$  |
L276: 
L277: In particular, if $S_{\alpha}\subseteq X_{0}$, this gives the non-relative Whitney (a)-condition (cite64†2.5 ).
L278: The existence of Thom’s $a_{\pi}$-stratifications for morphisms mapping to smooth curves goes back to Hironaka [cite50†35 , Sec. 5, Corollary 1]. In our setting, this condition simplifies considerably. Indeed, any stratification of the map $\pi$ in the sense of Definition cite65†2.6 will satisfy Thom’s $a_{\pi}$-condition. Let $\mathcal{S}$ be such a Whitney stratification of $\pi:\mathcal{X}\to\mathbb{A}^{1}$.
L279: Since $\pi$ is projective, hence proper, Thom’s first isotopy lemma [cite66†63 ] implies that the restriction $\pi|_{S}:S\to\pi(S)$ is a locally trivial fibration for every stratum $S\in\mathcal{S}$. The theorem of Briançon-Maisonobe-Merle [cite67†8 , Theorem 4.2.1] then implies that $\mathcal{S}$ satisfies Thom’s $a_{\pi}$-condition.
L280: Moreover, for Gröbner degenerations, it is enough to use the usual Whitney stratification (in the sense of Definition cite64†2.5 ) of $\mathcal{X}$ compatible with $X_{0}$, as shown in the following lemma.
L281: ###### Lemma 3.9.
L282: 
L283: Let $\mathcal{X}\to\mathbb{A}^{1}$ be a Gröbner degeneration, and let $\mathcal{S}$ be the minimal Whitney stratification of $\mathcal{X}$ compatible with the special fiber $X_{0}$. Then a Whitney stratification of the map $\pi:\mathcal{X}\to\mathbb{A}^{1}$ is given by $\mathcal{S}$ and the stratification $\{\mathbb{A}^{1}\setminus\{0\},\{0\}\}$ of the line $\mathbb{A}^{1}$.
L284: ###### Proof.
L285: We have to show that for every stratum $S$ of $\mathcal{S}$, the map $\pi|_{S}$ is a submersion onto the corresponding stratum of $\{\mathbb{A}^{1}\setminus\{0\},\{0\}\}$. Since $\mathcal{S}$ is compatible with $X_{0}$, every stratum is either contained in $X_{0}$ or disjoint from $X_{0}$.
L286: As in the proof of Proposition cite30†3.3 , one can show that a Gröbner degeneration is equivariantly trivial over the punctured line $\mathbb{A}^{1}\setminus\{0\}$, meaning, $\mathcal{X}^{\times}:=\mathcal{X}\cap\pi^{-1}(\mathbb{C}^{\times})\simeq X\times\mathbb{C}^{\times}$. Under this trivialization, the $\mathbb{C}^{\times}$-action is given by
L287:  | $$\rho_{\lambda}:\mathcal{X}\to\mathcal{X},\hskip 10.00002pt(x,t)\mapsto(\lambda^{\omega}\cdot x,\lambda t),\hskip 10.00002pt\lambda\in\mathbb{C}^{\times}.$$  |
L288: We claim that the automorphisms $\rho_{\lambda}$ preserve the restricted stratification $\mathcal{S}|_{\mathcal{X}^{\times}}$. Indeed, viewing $\rho_{\lambda}$ as a diffeomorphism of the underlying analytic space, the image of $\mathcal{S}$ is again a Whitney stratification by [cite54†27 , p. 11]. Since each $\rho_{\lambda}$ preserves the special fiber $X_{0}$, the image stratification $\rho_{\lambda}(\mathcal{S})$ is again compatible with $X_{0}$.
L289: By uniqueness of the minimal Whitney stratification compatible with $X_{0}$, the action therefore permutes the strata of $\mathcal{S}|_{\mathcal{X}}^{\times}$.
L290: There are only finitely many such strata and $\mathbb{C}^{\times}$ is connected, thus, each stratum $S\subset\mathcal{X}^{\times}$ is in fact fixed, and therefore has the form $S=S_{1}\times\mathbb{C}^{\times}$, where $S_{1}=S\cap(X\times\{1\})$. On such a stratum, the map $\pi$ is just the projection to $\mathbb{C}^{\times}$, therefore $\pi|_{S}$ is a submersion. The remaining strata are contained in $X_{0}$.
L291: They map to the point $\{0\}$, and the differential to the tangent space of a point is automatically surjective. Thus $\pi$ is a stratified submersion. ∎
L292: ###### Remark 3.10.
L293: 
L294: A stratum of $\mathcal{X}$ will be called vertical if it is contained in a single fiber of $\pi$. The proof of the lemma above shows that, for the chosen minimal Whitney stratification of a Gröbner degeneration, the only vertical strata are those contained in the special fiber $X_{0}$.
L295: The following result makes the source of the extra components precise: after choosing a Whitney stratification of the map, compatible with the special fiber, every irreducible component of the limiting conormal cycle comes from one of the strata contained in the special fiber.
L296: ###### Theorem 3.11.
L297: 
L298: Let $\mathcal{X}\to\mathbb{A}^{1}$ be a flat Gröbner degeneration, and let $\mathcal{S}$ be the minimal Whitney stratification of $\mathcal{X}$ compatible with $X_{0}$. Then every irreducible component $W$ of the reduced special fiber $(\mathcal{N}_{\mathcal{X}/\mathbb{A}^{1}})_{0}^{\mathrm{red}}$ is the conormal variety of a stratum contained in $X_{0}$, i.e.,
